title: Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?
outcomes: Names the loose pieces of either side
Takes a loose piece, the one with the higher counting value first
Checks for a far-away defender before calling a piece free
Says when there is nothing to take

steps.text: Your rook just took a knight, and Black could not take back. In this course that knight was **loose**: an enemy piece attacked it, and none of its own side's pieces defended it. A loose piece can be taken for free. Missing a free piece, yours or theirs, is one of the most common ways a game swings. [H] I suspect it is the most common cause below club level, but I have not measured it.

steps.caption: The rook looks up the d-file at a knight that has no friend beside it or behind it.

line.say: The rook takes the knight. No black piece guards d5, so nothing can take the rook back.
Black has no recapture. A whole knight is gone for nothing.

claims.statement: Only the knight on d5 is loose.
No black piece defends the knight.
Taking the knight wins it for nothing.

steps.caption: Same rook, same knight, but now a pawn on e6 defends it. Attacked is not the same as loose.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
The pawn takes back. White gave a rook for a knight, a bad trade.

claims.statement: No black piece is loose.
The pawn on e6 defends the knight.
Taking the knight loses the rook for a knight.

steps.text: In this course a piece is **loose** when two things are true: an enemy piece **attacks** it, and no friendly piece **defends** it. Attacked but defended is not loose: they take back. Many coaches call any undefended piece loose and use *hanging* for the attacked kind [R: recalled usage, no source read]. We keep the two states apart. Undefended but not attacked is not free yet, and the next board shows why it still matters.

steps.caption: [I] Nothing is loose yet, but the rook on b4 and the bishop on f6 are both undefended. One knight move attacks both: undefended pieces are the targets of double attacks.

line.say: The knight jumps to d5 and attacks the rook and the bishop at once. Neither has a guard.
Black saves the rook.
The knight takes the bishop with check.

claims.statement: Before the move no black piece is loose.
After the knight move both are loose.
The fork is the engine's best move.

steps.caption: Three black pieces to sort. Bishop: attacked, no guard, so loose. Knight: attacked but guarded. Rook: no guard, but not attacked.

line.say: The pawn takes the bishop. Nothing guards g4, so nothing takes the pawn back.

claims.statement: Only the bishop on g4 is loose.
The pawn on e6 defends the knight.
Nothing attacks the rook on a8.
Taking the bishop is the engine's best move.

steps.caption: Any piece can be the attacker, even a pawn. Here the pawn attacks a knight that no black piece guards.

line.say: A pawn is worth little, yet it takes the knight. Nothing recaptures.
White has won a whole knight for nothing.

claims.statement: The knight on d6 is loose.
Taking the knight is the engine's best move.

steps.text: Sometimes two pieces are loose at once, and you can take only one now. A good default is to take the **higher-value** piece first, then see whether the other can run. [I] That default comes from these two boards, not from a law. Both orders are shown, so you can compare. Two boards after them show when the order matters less.

steps.caption: Two loose pieces: the rook on b8, attacked by the bishop, and the knight on d4, attacked by the rook.

line.say: The bishop takes the bigger prize, the rook. The knight is still attacked.
Black rescues the knight, but the rook is gone for good.

claims.statement: Both the rook and the knight are loose.
Taking the rook first is the engine's best move.

steps.caption: The other order: the rook takes the knight first.

line.say: The rook takes the knight first. Now the black rook on b8 is still attacked.
The black rook runs. White won only the knight.

claims.statement: Taking the knight first wins only the knight.
It is worse than taking the rook first.

steps.text: The default bends when the smaller piece cannot run. A knight **pinned** to its king cannot move, so both orders win both pieces. [I] The reverse case: if the bigger piece cannot run but the smaller one can, take the smaller one first, before it escapes. Always ask which piece can actually get away.

steps.caption: The knight on d4 is pinned to its king by the rook, so it cannot run. Take the bigger prize first.

line.say: The bishop takes the rook.
The king leaves the file, but it is White's move: the knight is taken before it can run.
The rook takes the knight. Both pieces are won.

claims.statement: Both the knight and the rook are loose.
Either capture is among the engine's best moves.

steps.caption: The other order also works: the rook takes the pinned knight with check, so the king must answer and cannot guard the rook.

line.say: The rook takes the knight and gives check.
The king steps out of check.
The bishop takes the rook. Both pieces are won.

claims.statement: Both the knight and the rook are loose.
Either capture is among the engine's best moves.

steps.text: Your own pieces can be loose too. After **every** move your opponent makes, check two lists: their loose pieces and yours. [H] My guess is that players miss their own loose pieces more than the enemy's, because after your own move your mind is on your plan. [I] An unchecked scan fails most often on your own side. I have not measured either.

steps.caption: Both lists on one board. Their loose piece: the bishop on g4, attacked by the h3 pawn. Yours: the rook on d1, attacked by that bishop.

claims.statement: The bishop on g4 is loose.
The rook on d1 is loose.

steps.caption: Best answer: take the attacker. One capture wins their piece and ends the danger to yours.

line.say: The pawn takes the bishop. Nothing attacks the rook on d1 any more.

claims.statement: The pawn wins the bishop.
No white piece is loose afterwards.

steps.caption: Now you cannot capture the bishop. Black has just moved it to g4, attacking your undefended rook. Fix one: move the piece away.

line.say: The rook steps to a square the bishop does not attack.

claims.statement: The rook on d1 is loose.
No white piece is loose after the rook moves.

steps.caption: Fix two: block the line. A piece between the bishop and the rook stops the attack.

line.say: The pawn blocks the bishop's line. The bishop now attacks the pawn, and the g2 pawn guards it.

claims.statement: No white piece is loose after the block.
The pawn on g2 defends f3.

steps.caption: The answer to the last task, as a fix. The bishop on c4 is attacked and undefended, so it must move.

line.say: The bishop retreats to a square the knight on d6 does not attack.

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 is loose.
No white piece is loose after the retreat.

steps.caption: Fix three: defend the piece. A pawn on b3 guards the bishop, so a knight capture would be answered by a recapture.

line.say: The pawn guards the bishop on c4.
If the knight takes anyway...
...the pawn takes back: bishop for knight, an even trade.

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 is loose before the move.
No white piece is loose after the defence.

steps.text: Your answers to an attacked piece: **capture** the attacker, **move** away, **block** the line, **defend** the piece, or **counterattack** with a bigger threat. Defending works well when the attacker is worth as much as your piece or more. A cheaper attacker, such as a bishop against a rook, still wins value even against a defended piece. A counterattack must really be bigger.

A loose piece is free only if no defender can take back, and a defender can stand far away. A rook or queen guards along a whole file or row. A bishop or queen guards along a whole diagonal. A knight guards by its jump, a pawn the two squares diagonally ahead of it, and the king the squares beside it. Before you capture, trace lines back from the piece. Here is a defender that is easy to miss.

steps.caption: The bishop in the corner is far from the knight, but nothing stands between them on the long diagonal.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
The bishop takes back from across the board. White lost a rook for a knight.

claims.statement: No black piece is loose.
The bishop on a8 defends the knight.
Taking the knight loses the rook for a knight.

steps.caption: A rook standing behind the piece guards it just as well. Here the rook on d8 defends the knight.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
The other rook takes back along the file. Rook for knight.

claims.statement: The rook on d8 defends the knight.
Taking the knight loses a rook for a knight.

steps.text: A defender can also fail while it still stands there. Edward Lasker's *Chess Strategy* names three ways: a cheaper piece can capture the defender, a bigger threat elsewhere can pull it away, or it can be **pinned** (my paraphrase, from our reading notes). Look at a pinned one: it guards on paper but cannot take back.

steps.caption: Defended on paper. The bishop on e6 guards the knight, but the rook on e1 pins it to the king, so it cannot take back.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
Black cannot recapture: the pinned bishop may not leave the e-file.

claims.statement: On paper the bishop on e6 defends the knight.
The rook still wins the knight.
Taking the knight is the engine's best move.

steps.text: The second question is what the capture costs. A piece that guards something important may be needed where it stands. Look at the first row of the next board: White's rook is the only piece keeping the king safe.

steps.caption: The knight is loose, but White's king has no flight square: its own pawns block the second row.

line.say: The rook takes the knight and leaves the first row.
Black's rook lands on the first row. The king cannot move or capture: checkmate.

claims.statement: The knight on d5 is loose.
Taking the knight is a serious mistake.

steps.caption: The position after the capture, Black to move. One rook move ends the game.

line.say: The rook gives check on the first row. Nothing can block or capture, and the king has no square.

claims.statement: Re1 is checkmate.

steps.caption: With a pawn on h3, the king has the square h2. The rook can take the knight safely.

line.say: The rook takes the knight.
Black checks on the first row.
The king steps to h2, off the first row. The check is answered.

claims.statement: The rook wins the knight.
The king can step to h2.

steps.caption: Another duty. The rook on a3 is the only guard of the bishop on c3. The knight on a6 looks free, but the rook has a job.

line.say: The rook takes the knight and stops guarding the bishop.
The black bishop takes the bishop. The free knight was only an even trade.

claims.statement: The knight on a6 is loose.
Taking the knight is worse than the engine's best move.

steps.text: Two questions before every capture. **Is any piece defending it, even from far away, or only on paper?** **What does my capturing piece stop doing, and what is my opponent's most forcing reply: a check, a capture or a threat?** That scan has its own lesson in the loop course. If the answers are no and nothing, the piece really is free. Then a case where a defender exists, but the capture is still good.

steps.caption: The rook on d8 defends the knight, so it is not loose. But the capturer is only a pawn.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight.
The rook takes the pawn. White gave a pawn (1) for a knight (3).

claims.statement: The knight is not loose.
The rook on d8 defends the knight.
White comes out two points ahead.

steps.text: So **defended** means *not free*, but not always *safe to leave alone*: a cheap piece can attack an expensive defended one. Rule of thumb, from the counting values. A later lesson makes this exact by counting every attacker and defender. For now, one more fact. Attacking a loose piece does not win it if your opponent can move it.

steps.caption: Nothing is attacked yet. White attacks the knight, then it is Black's turn.

line.say: The rook attacks the knight, which is now loose. But it is Black's move.
The knight runs to a safe square. Nothing was won.

claims.statement: After the rook move the knight is loose.
Attacking the knight does not win it.

steps.caption: Often there is nothing to take. A common English-style move order, replayed with python-chess: after these six moves no piece on either side is loose.

line.say: White brings a knight out toward the centre.
Black mirrors with a knight.
A pawn grabs space and guards d5.
Black prepares to develop a bishop on the long diagonal.
A second knight comes out, defended by the b2 pawn.
The bishop takes the long diagonal.

claims.statement: No white piece is loose after six moves.
No black piece is loose after six moves.

steps.title: Same attack, one change
steps.prompt: Predict first: does Black win a piece in each position?

steps.text: A habit, as a rule of thumb. After each opponent move: **list their loose pieces, list yours, then count defenders before you take.** A loose piece is free on your move, not after you only attack it. Now the tests give no hints about which idea to use, and sometimes nothing is free.

Two named views, rephrased. Edward Lasker's *Chess Strategy* treats a defender as something that must itself be checked: it can be captured, pulled away or pinned. Znosko-Borovsky's *The Middle Game in Chess* separates threats that really win something from ones that would gain nothing if carried out (both from our reading notes, [S]). [I] My conjecture: the scan fails most often on your own pieces.

steps.prompt: Explain in your own words, as if to a friend: what makes a piece loose, and what are the two questions to ask before you capture one? Then compare with the model answer on the next card.

steps.text: **Model answer.** A piece is loose when an enemy piece attacks it and none of its own side defends it. After every move I check both sides, and I trace long lines for far-away defenders. Before I take, I ask whether a defender is real, and what my capturing piece stops doing.

steps.prompt: Think of a game you lost material in. Which of your pieces was in danger, and what would you check first next time?
